glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Faith in the Lord of glory refuses favoritism, keeps the royal law of love, shows mercy, and proves itself alive by what it does, as the needy brother or sister, Abraham, and Rahab make plain.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: James 2 completes the movement that began with “be doers of the word” (1:22). The scene of a rich visitor and a poor one entering the believers’ assembly puts the call to care for the vulnerable (1:27) to a concrete test.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “Thus also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.” (James 2:17)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
James begins with a scene any congregation would recognize. A man with gold rings is shown to a good seat, while a poor man in filthy clothes is told to stand or sit on the floor (2:2–3). James calls this a contradiction of “the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory” (2:1). God has chosen the poor of this world “to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom” (2:5), yet the church has dishonored them while courting the very people who oppress it.

Partiality breaks the royal law, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (2:8), and the same God who gave that command gave every other one, so no one can excuse favoritism by pointing to the commands he keeps (2:10–11). Believers must speak and act as those who will be judged, “For judgment is without mercy to the one who has shown no mercy” (2:13). A settled refusal of mercy exposes a profession that will not stand before God, while mercy shown to others gives evidence of a life God has changed.

That warning leads straight into James’s question: “if someone says he has faith but does not have works,” can that faith save him (2:14)? Kind words to a brother or sister without food or clothing feed no one. Even demons believe that God is one, and they tremble (2:19). Abraham believed God and was counted righteous long before he offered Isaac, and that costly obedience showed his faith to be real and brought it to maturity (2:21–23). Rahab’s protection of the messengers likewise showed her faith to be real (2:25). Faith and works belong together as surely as body and spirit (2:26).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
James 2:1–7 — Partiality in the Assembly Dishonors the Poor

James forbids believers to treat people by their wealth, as when the man with gold rings receives a good seat and the poor man is told to stand. God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith and heirs of His kingdom, so dishonoring them sets the church against God’s own choice and toward the rich who oppress it.

James 2:8–13 — The Royal Law and Mercy at Judgment

Partiality breaks the command to love your neighbor as yourself and makes a person a lawbreaker before the God who gave every command. Believers must speak and act as people who will be judged, because judgment is merciless to the merciless, while mercy triumphs over judgment.

James 2:14–17 — A Claimed Faith That Leaves the Needy Unhelped

James asks whether a faith that produces no works can save. Wishing a hungry, poorly clothed brother or sister well without meeting their need does them no good, and faith that does nothing is just as dead.

James 2:18–20 — Faith Shown by Works, Not Mere Belief

Faith that is real can be shown by what it does. Even the demons believe that God is one and tremble, so correct belief alone cannot take the place of trusting obedience.

James 2:21–24 — Abraham’s Faith Made Perfect by Works

Abraham’s offering of Isaac showed that the faith God had already counted as righteousness was genuine. His faith worked together with his obedience and was brought to maturity, so James concludes that a person is justified by works and not by a faith that never acts.

James 2:25–26 — Rahab and the Body Without the Spirit

Rahab showed the reality of her faith when she welcomed and protected Israel’s messengers. James ends the argument with a picture: as a body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
James 2 shows that the way a church treats a poor visitor is a matter of honoring the Lord of glory. Seating, attention, and help reveal what believers really value, and James counts favoritism as sin against God’s law of love (2:1, 9).

The chapter also clarifies how faith and works belong together. Abraham was counted righteous through faith before he offered Isaac (Genesis 15:6; 22:1–18), and his obedience showed that faith to be real. James agrees with Paul’s teaching that God declares the ungodly righteous through faith (Romans 4:1–5). He exposes a claim to faith that never acts, and he leaves no room either for earning salvation by mercy or for resting in a barren profession.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
No partiality. Faith in the Lord of glory rules out favoring the rich and dishonoring the poor (2:1–7).

The royal law. Love for neighbor is God’s standard, and every command comes from the same God (2:8–11).

Mercy and judgment. Settled mercilessness meets judgment without mercy, and mercy shown to others triumphs over judgment (2:12–13).

Living and dead faith. A faith that leaves the needy unhelped is dead, while living faith acts (2:14–17, 26).

Faith made perfect. Abraham’s and Rahab’s actions showed their faith to be genuine (2:21–25).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
The Lord of glory (2:1). A title for Jesus that places Him above every human rank. Honoring people by their clothing contradicts faith in Him.

Assembly (2:2). The Greek word is the common word for a synagogue, a Jewish meeting place. Here it describes the gathering of Jewish believers in Jesus.

The royal law (2:8). The command “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18), which James calls royal because it is the King’s law.

The law of liberty (2:12). God’s word, which frees His people for obedient love and also holds their words and actions accountable. James first used the phrase in 1:25.

Justified by works (2:21, 24). In James’s argument, genuine faith shown to be real through obedience. Abraham was counted righteous when he believed God (Genesis 15:6), and his later obedience displayed and matured that faith.

Rahab the harlot (2:25). The woman of Jericho who hid Israel’s spies and confessed that their God was God in heaven above and on earth beneath (Joshua 2:8–13). James commends her actions in protecting the messengers.

focus: James 2 tests whether the faith of “our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory” (James 2:1) is held without partiality and shows itself in mercy and obedient action. James exposes favoritism toward the rich as a breach of the royal law, warns that judgment is without mercy to the merciless, and shows through the needy brother or sister, Abraham, and Rahab that faith without works is dead.

sections.title: Partiality in the Assembly Dishonors the Poor
sections.summary: James forbids his brethren to hold their faith in the Lord of glory with partiality, as when they give the man with gold rings a good seat and tell the poor man to stand. God has chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, yet the church has dishonored the poor man, while the rich oppress the believers and blaspheme the noble name by which they are called.

sections.title: The Royal Law and Mercy at Judgment
sections.summary: Fulfilling the royal law, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (James 2:8), rules out partiality, which convicts people as transgressors of the whole law, since the same God gave every command. Believers must speak and act as those who will be judged by the law of liberty, for “judgment is without mercy to the one who has shown no mercy” (James 2:13).

sections.title: A Claimed Faith That Leaves the Needy Unhelped
sections.summary: James asks what profit there is if someone says he has faith but does not have works, and whether that faith can save him. Words of blessing to a brother or sister without clothing or daily food meet no need, and “faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead” (James 2:17).

sections.title: Faith Shown by Works, Not Mere Belief
sections.summary: The exchange presses the demand that faith be shown by works, since even the demons believe that there is one God and tremble. James then asks the foolish man whether he wants to know “that faith without works is dead” (James 2:20).

sections.title: Abraham’s Faith Made Perfect by Works
sections.summary: Abraham was justified by works when he offered Isaac his son on the altar, for faith was working together with his works, and by works faith was made perfect. The Scripture that says “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness” (James 2:23) was fulfilled, and James concludes that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only.

sections.title: Rahab and the Body Without the Spirit
sections.summary: Rahab the harlot was likewise justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out another way. James closes the argument with a comparison: “as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also” (James 2:26).

1.brief: James tells his brethren not to hold “the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with partiality.” Faith in the glorious Lord cannot sit alongside favoritism based on wealth or outward rank.
1.explain:
“My brethren, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with partiality.”

James begins a new subject with a command. Believers must not hold their faith “with partiality.” Partiality means favoritism, treating people differently because of outward appearance, wealth, or social rank.

The faith they hold is “the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ.” James calls Jesus “the Lord of glory.” All glory belongs to Him. Compared with His glory, the differences between rich and poor shrink to nothing. To honor someone because of gold rings and fine clothes while trusting the Lord of glory is a contradiction. Faith in the glorious Lord cannot sit alongside favoritism based on wealth or outward rank.
1.notes:
The Greek word translated “partiality” is formed from words meaning to receive a face. It describes judging people by outward appearance. Paul uses the same word for God, who shows no partiality (Romans 2:11).

The Greek construction behind “the Lord of glory” can also be read as our glorious Lord Jesus Christ. Either way, the glory belongs to Jesus.

2.brief: James pictures two visitors coming into the assembly: a man with gold rings and fine apparel, and a poor man in filthy clothes. The scene sets up a test of how the church receives people.
2.explain:
“For if there should come into your assembly a man with gold rings, in fine apparel,”

James gives an example. A visitor comes “into your assembly,” the gathering of believers. He is “a man with gold rings, in fine apparel.” His jewelry and clothing announce his wealth and status.

“and there should also come in a poor man in filthy clothes,”

Another visitor comes: “a poor man in filthy clothes.” His clothing is shabby and dirty. Everything about his appearance signals poverty. The scene sets up a test of how the church receives people.
2.notes: The Greek word translated “assembly” is the word for “synagogue.” James uses it for the gathering of Jewish believers in Jesus. In 5:14 he uses the usual word for “church.”

3.brief: If the church pays special attention to the well-dressed man and says, “You sit here in a good place,” while telling the poor man, “You stand there,” or to sit at someone’s footstool, it honors wealth and slights poverty. The seating itself announces who the church thinks matters.
3.explain:
“and you pay attention to the one wearing the fine clothes”

The church gives the rich man special treatment. They notice him, look at him with favor, and go out of their way to welcome him. Their attention is drawn by his clothing.

“and say to him, ‘You sit here in a good place,”

They tell him, “You sit here in a good place.” He is given a comfortable, honored seat.

“and say to the poor man, ‘You stand there,’ or, ‘Sit here at my footstool,”

The poor man receives different treatment. He is told, “You stand there,” or “Sit here at my footstool.” He gets no seat at all, or he is sent to the floor beside someone’s feet. The seating itself announces who the church thinks matters.
3.notes: The Greek verb translated “pay attention” means to look upon with favor or regard. It describes more than noticing someone.

4.brief: Giving the rich man the good seat and sending the poor man to stand or sit on the floor shows partiality among believers and makes them “judges with evil thoughts.” Believers who rank people by wealth become judges whose verdicts rest on corrupt reasoning.
4.explain:
“have you not shown partiality among yourselves,”

James asks a question that answers itself, and the answer is yes. They have made distinctions that contradict their faith.

“and become judges with evil thoughts?”

They have taken the place of judges, deciding who deserves honor and who does not. Their verdicts rest on “evil thoughts,” corrupt reasoning that measures people by wealth. Believers who rank people by wealth become judges whose verdicts rest on corrupt reasoning.
4.notes: The Greek verb translated “shown partiality” is the same verb translated “doubting” in 1:6. It can mean to make distinctions or to be divided. Some take James to mean that partiality shows a divided mind, the same instability he condemned in 1:6–8.

5.brief: James calls his beloved brethren to listen: God has “chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom” He promised to those who love Him. Treating the poor with contempt sets the church against God’s own choice.
5.explain:
“Listen, my beloved brethren:”

James calls for attention. “Listen,” he says to his “beloved brethren.” What follows exposes how badly they have misjudged.

“Has God not chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith”

James asks another question that expects a yes. “Has God not chosen the poor of this world?” God has often chosen people the world overlooks. The poor are “poor” in the eyes of “this world,” but God has made them “rich in faith.” Their real wealth is their trust in Him.

“and heirs of the kingdom which He promised to those who love Him?”

God has also made them “heirs of the kingdom.” They will inherit God’s kingdom, the kingdom “He promised to those who love Him.” The same promise was attached to the crown of life in 1:12.

God honors the poor whom the church has dishonored. Treating the poor with contempt sets the church against God’s own choice. Poverty does not earn salvation, and wealth does not prove unbelief. But God’s choice exposes how foolish it is to rank people by money.
5.notes: Jesus said, “Blessed are you poor, For yours is the kingdom of God” (Luke 6:20). Paul writes that God has chosen “the foolish things of the world to put to shame the wise” (1 Corinthians 1:27).

6.brief: “But you have dishonored the poor man,” James says, even though it is the rich who oppress believers and drag them into the courts. The church is courting the favor of people who mistreat it.
6.explain:
“But you have dishonored the poor man.”

“But” brings a sharp contrast. God has honored the poor, “but you have dishonored the poor man.” The church has done the opposite of what God did. By sending the poor man to stand or sit on the floor, they treated him with contempt.

“Do not the rich oppress you and drag you into the courts?”

James points out another irony. “Do not the rich oppress you?” The rich, as a group, were the ones mistreating believers. They “drag you into the courts,” using their power and the legal system against the poor. The church is courting the favor of people who mistreat it.

James is speaking of the rich as a class known to his readers, not of every wealthy person. He does not describe a particular lawsuit.
6.notes: The Greek verb translated “oppress” means to exercise power over someone harshly. It is used in Acts 10:38 of those “oppressed by the devil.”

7.brief: The rich oppressors James has just described “blaspheme that noble name by which you are called.” Showing them favor means honoring those who speak against the name of the Lord that believers bear.
7.explain:
“Do they not blaspheme that noble name by which you are called?”

James adds a third question. “Do they not blaspheme that noble name?” The rich oppressors speak against “that noble name,” the name of Jesus Christ. It is the name “by which you are called,” the name believers bear because they belong to Him.

Showing favor to those who speak against the name of the Lord dishonors the Lord whose name believers carry.
7.notes: The phrase “by which you are called” reads literally which was called upon you. In the Old Testament, having God’s name called over someone marked that person as belonging to Him (for example, Amos 9:12, where nations are “called by My name”).

8.brief: Believers do well when they really fulfill the royal law of Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Love for one’s neighbor is the standard that partiality breaks.
8.explain:
“If you really fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture,”

James turns from what believers must not do to what they must do. He speaks of “the royal law.” It is royal because it comes from God the King and because it rules over all the other commands that concern how people treat one another. It is found “according to the Scripture,” in God’s written word.

“You shall love your neighbor as yourself,’ you do well;”

The royal law is “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” James quotes Leviticus 19:18. Jesus called this the second great commandment (Matthew 22:39). If believers “really fulfill” this law, they “do well.” Love for one’s neighbor is the standard that partiality breaks. The poor man in filthy clothes was a neighbor, and he should have been loved as the church loved itself.
8.notes:
Leviticus 19:15, a few verses before the command to love one’s neighbor, forbids partiality in judgment: “You shall not be partial to the poor, nor honor the person of the mighty.”

The Greek word translated “royal” means belonging to a king.

9.brief: Showing partiality is sin, and those who do it are “convicted by the law as transgressors.” Favoritism breaks God’s law, and the law itself exposes the offender.
9.explain:
“but if you show partiality, you commit sin,”

James states the opposite case plainly. Favoritism is not a social mistake or a matter of manners. It is sin.

“and are convicted by the law as transgressors.”

The law itself exposes them as lawbreakers. The same Scripture that commands love for one’s neighbor condemns partiality (Leviticus 19:15). Favoritism breaks God’s law, and the law itself exposes the offender.
9.notes: The Greek verb translated “convicted” means to expose or prove guilty. It is used in John 16:8 for the Spirit who “will convict the world of sin.”

10.brief: Whoever keeps the whole law yet stumbles in one point “is guilty of all.” God’s law stands as a single whole, so a person cannot excuse partiality by pointing to the commands he keeps.
10.explain:
“For whoever shall keep the whole law,”

James explains why partiality is so serious. He imagines someone who “shall keep the whole law,” obeying every command but one.

“and yet stumble in one point, he is guilty of all.”

The law is not a list of separate rules that a person can pick from. It is a single whole, given by one God. Breaking any part of it makes a person a lawbreaker.

This does not mean that every sin is equally serious, or that breaking one command is the same as breaking every command. It means that a person cannot excuse partiality by pointing to all the commands he keeps. God’s law stands as a single whole.
10.notes: The Greek verb translated “stumble” is used again in 3:2: “For we all stumble in many things.”

11.brief: The same God who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” A person who avoids adultery but commits murder still becomes a transgressor of the law, because every command comes from the one God who gave them all.
11.explain:
“For He who said, ‘Do not commit adultery,’ also said, ‘Do not murder.”

James gives an example. The God who commanded against adultery also commanded against murder. Both commands come from the same Lawgiver (Exodus 20:13–14).

“Now if you do not commit adultery, but you do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law.”

A person might avoid adultery but commit murder. He cannot claim to be law-abiding because of the one command he kept. He has “become a transgressor of the law.” Every command comes from the one God who gave them all. The same is true of partiality. A person cannot excuse favoritism by pointing to the commands he keeps.
11.notes: James names adultery before murder. Jesus and Paul also list these two commands in that order (Luke 18:20; Romans 13:9).

12.brief: Believers are to “speak and so do as those who will be judged by the law of liberty.” Their words and actions answer to God’s word, which frees them for obedient love and holds them accountable.
12.explain:
“So speak and so do as those who will be judged by the law of liberty.”

James draws a conclusion. Believers must “speak” and “do,” in both words and actions, “as those who will be judged by the law of liberty.” They will give account to God for how they have lived.

“The law of liberty” is the same law James described in 1:25: God’s word, which frees His people for obedient love. It frees them, but it also holds them accountable. Their words and actions answer to God’s word. Freedom does not mean exemption from judgment.
12.notes: The phrase “speak and so do” brings together the two areas James addresses throughout the letter: speech (1:19, 26; 3:1–12) and action (1:22–25; 2:14–26).

13.brief: “Judgment is without mercy to the one who has shown no mercy,” yet “mercy triumphs over judgment.” A settled refusal to show mercy exposes a profession of faith that will not stand at the final judgment, while mercy shown to others gives evidence of a life transformed by God and confidence before Him.
13.explain:
“For judgment is without mercy to the one who has shown no mercy.”

James explains why the coming judgment matters. A person who has refused to show mercy to others will face God’s judgment without mercy.

This is a severe warning. The person James describes has a settled pattern of mercilessness. A settled refusal to show mercy exposes a profession of faith that will not stand at the final judgment. James addresses the church, so the warning also calls genuine believers who have shown favoritism to repent and act mercifully.

“Mercy triumphs over judgment.”

James ends with a ringing statement. Mercy wins. The immediate emphasis falls on the mercy believers show to others. Such mercy gives evidence of a life transformed by God and gives confidence before Him on the day of judgment. Showing mercy does not purchase salvation. God’s mercy in Christ is the ground of salvation, and the mercy His people show is the evidence that they have received it.
13.notes:
Jesus said, “Blessed are the merciful, For they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7). His parable of the unforgiving servant warns against refusing mercy after receiving it (Matthew 18:21–35).

The Greek verb translated “triumphs” means to boast over or prevail against.

14.brief: James asks what profit there is if someone “says he has faith but does not have works,” and whether that faith can save him. The implied answer is no: a claim to faith that produces no action cannot save, because genuine faith shows itself in mercy and obedience.
14.explain:
“What does it profit, my brethren,”

James begins a new section with a question: “What does it profit?” What good is it? He is about to describe a faith that accomplishes nothing.

“if someone says he has faith but does not have works?”

James describes “someone” who “says he has faith.” The key word is “says.” This person claims to have faith. But he “does not have works.” His claim is not matched by any action.

“Can faith save him?”

The Greek wording expects the answer no. The faith in question is the kind just described, a faith that is claimed but produces no works. Such a faith cannot save. James is not saying that faith in Christ is insufficient for salvation. He is saying that a faith that never acts is not genuine saving faith at all. Genuine faith shows itself in mercy and obedience.
14.notes: The Greek question “Can faith save him?” uses a form that expects a negative answer. Many translations bring out the reference to the faith just described by asking whether that faith can save him.

15.brief: James imagines a brother or sister who is “naked and destitute of daily food.” The example sets the argument within a situation of real and urgent need in the church family.
15.explain:
“If a brother or sister is naked and destitute of daily food,”

James gives an example. A “brother or sister,” a fellow believer, is “naked and destitute of daily food.” “Naked” means poorly clothed, lacking adequate clothing. “Destitute of daily food” means not having enough to eat each day. This is real, urgent need in the church family.
15.notes: The Greek word translated “naked” often means poorly or inadequately clothed rather than wearing nothing at all.

16.brief: If one of the believers tells that brother or sister without clothing or food, “Depart in peace, be warmed and filled,” but gives them nothing their bodies need, the words do them no good. Religious kindness that offers words alone leaves the needy as cold and hungry as before.
16.explain:
“and one of you says to them, ‘Depart in peace, be warmed and filled,”

A believer meets this needy brother or sister and “says to them, ‘Depart in peace, be warmed and filled.’” The words sound kind and even religious. “Depart in peace” was a common farewell blessing. “Be warmed and filled” wishes them warmth and food.

“but you do not give them the things which are needed for the body,”

But the believer does not give them “the things which are needed for the body.” He offers no clothing, no food, no help. His words cost him nothing.

“what does it profit?”

What good do the words do? None. The needy person is just as cold and hungry as before. Religious kindness that offers words alone leaves the needy as cold and hungry as before.
16.notes: John makes the same point: “But whoever has this world’s goods, and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his heart from him, how does the love of God abide in him?” (1 John 3:17).

17.brief: In the same way, faith by itself, if it does not have works, “is dead.” A faith that never acts is lifeless, as empty as the blessing spoken to the hungry.
17.explain:
“Thus also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.”

James applies the example. The empty words of 2:16 helped no one. A faith that never acts is equally empty. It is not alive. It is “dead.”

A dead faith is a faith in name only. It may say the right words, but it has no life in it. Living faith produces works the way a living tree produces fruit. A faith that never acts is lifeless, as empty as the blessing spoken to the hungry.
17.notes: The phrase “by itself” means faith alone, existing without any works accompanying it.

18.brief: James introduces someone who says, “You have faith, and I have works,” and the verse presses the challenge: “Show me your faith without your works, and I will show you my faith by my works.” Faith that is genuine can be seen in what a person does.
18.explain:
“But someone will say, ‘You have faith, and I have works.”

James introduces an imagined speaker who says, “You have faith, and I have works.” This speaker seems to suggest that faith and works can be separated, as if some people have the gift of faith and others the gift of works.

“Show me your faith without your works, and I will show you my faith by my works.”

James answers the challenge. “Show me your faith without your works.” It cannot be done. Faith is invisible unless it acts. Then James says, “I will show you my faith by my works.” Faith that is genuine can be seen in what a person does.
18.notes: The Greek text had no quotation marks, and interpreters disagree about where the imagined speaker’s words end in this verse. The NKJV ends the quotation after “I have works.” The difficulty does not change James’s main point: genuine faith cannot be separated from its expression in conduct.

19.brief: “You believe that there is one God. You do well.” Yet “even the demons believe—and tremble,” shaking with dread before the God they oppose, so correct belief about God can exist without trusting allegiance to Him.
19.explain:
“You believe that there is one God. You do well.”

James addresses someone who believes “that there is one God.” This is the most basic confession of Israel’s faith: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one!” (Deuteronomy 6:4). James affirms this belief. “You do well.” It is true.

“Even the demons believe—and tremble!”

But correct belief is not enough. “Even the demons believe.” They know there is one God. They know it better than many people do. And they “tremble,” shaking with dread before the God they oppose. Yet they remain His enemies.

Correct belief about God can exist without trusting allegiance to Him. Saving faith includes knowing the truth about God, but it goes further. It trusts Him, loves Him, and obeys Him.
19.notes: The Greek verb translated “tremble” means to shudder or bristle with fear. It appears only here in the New Testament.

20.brief: James rebukes the one who claims faith without works as “O foolish man” and asks whether he wants to know “that faith without works is dead.” The question introduces the proof from Scripture that follows in Abraham and Rahab.
20.explain:
“But do you want to know, O foolish man,”

James addresses his imagined opponent directly: “O foolish man.” “Foolish” means empty, hollow. The person who claims faith without works is as empty as the faith he claims.

“that faith without works is dead?”

James is about to give the proof from Scripture, in the examples of Abraham and Rahab.
20.notes: Some Greek manuscripts read “dead” in this verse, while many others read a word meaning “useless” or “idle.” The NKJV follows the reading “dead,” which matches 2:17 and 2:26.

21.brief: Abraham our father was “justified by works when he offered Isaac his son on the altar.” His costly obedience showed that the faith by which God had already counted him righteous was genuine.
21.explain:
“Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered Isaac his son on the altar?”

James turns to “Abraham our father,” the father of the Jewish people and the great example of faith. James asks a question that expects a yes: was not Abraham “justified by works when he offered Isaac his son on the altar?”

The event is recorded in Genesis 22:1–18. God told Abraham to offer Isaac as a sacrifice. Abraham obeyed, and God stopped him at the last moment and provided a ram instead.

Abraham’s costly obedience showed that the faith by which God had already counted him righteous was genuine. Years earlier, God had declared Abraham righteous because he believed (Genesis 15:6). When Abraham offered Isaac, his obedience proved that his faith was real. He was justified by works in the sense that his works demonstrated the genuineness of his faith.
21.notes: The Greek verb translated “offered” describes bringing something up to the altar. Abraham placed Isaac on the altar and took the knife, but God stopped him and provided a ram in Isaac’s place (Genesis 22:9–13).

22.brief: Abraham’s faith “was working together with his works, and by works faith was made perfect.” His obedience expressed the faith he already had and brought it to maturity.
22.explain:
“Do you see that faith was working together with his works,”

James asks, “Do you see?” Abraham’s faith “was working together with his works.” Faith and works were not separate or opposed. They worked as partners. Abraham’s faith led to his obedience, and his obedience expressed his faith.

“and by works faith was made perfect?”

“Perfect” means complete or mature. Abraham’s obedience brought his faith to maturity. His faith was genuine before he offered Isaac, but the test brought it to its full expression. His obedience expressed the faith he already had and brought it to maturity.
22.notes: The Greek verb translated “was made perfect” is related to the word “perfect” in 1:4. Tested faith, carried through, is brought to maturity.

23.brief: In this way the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness,” and he was called the friend of God. The offering of Isaac displayed the reality of the faith God had counted as righteousness long before Abraham went to the altar.
23.explain:
“And the Scripture was fulfilled which says, ‘Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.”

When Abraham offered Isaac, “the Scripture was fulfilled.” The Scripture James quotes is Genesis 15:6: “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.” God declared Abraham righteous because he believed. That declaration came years before the offering of Isaac.

When Abraham offered Isaac, that earlier Scripture was “fulfilled.” The offering of Isaac displayed the reality of the faith God had counted as righteousness long before Abraham went to the altar. The faith God had credited was shown to be real.

“And he was called the friend of God.”

The Old Testament gives Abraham this title (2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8). His trust and obedience showed a relationship of intimate friendship with God.
23.notes: Paul quotes the same verse, Genesis 15:6, in Romans 4:3.

24.brief: James concludes, “You see then that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only.” In context he means that genuine faith is shown to be real through obedience, and a claim to faith that never acts is not the faith that justifies.
24.explain:
“You see then that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only.”

James concludes: “a man is justified by works, and not by faith only.” This statement can seem to contradict Paul, who wrote, “a man is justified by faith apart from the deeds of the law” (Romans 3:28).

In context, James means that genuine faith is shown to be real through obedience. The “faith only” he rejects is the kind he has been describing: a faith that is claimed but never acts (2:14), a faith that offers empty words to the hungry (2:16), a faith like the demons’ belief (2:19). Such a faith does not justify. Paul and James agree that people are saved by grace through faith, and that genuine faith produces good works (Ephesians 2:8–10). Paul addresses those who try to earn salvation by works. James addresses those who claim faith but do not live it.

25.brief: Rahab the harlot was likewise “justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out another way.” Her protective actions gave visible expression to the allegiance to Israel’s God that she had confessed.
25.explain:
“Likewise, was not Rahab the harlot also justified by works”

James gives a second example: “Rahab the harlot.” She was a Canaanite woman in Jericho, a pagan by background and a prostitute by occupation. Abraham was the honored father of Israel. Rahab was an outsider with a shameful past. Yet both show the same truth.

Rahab was “also justified by works.” Like Abraham, her actions showed that her faith was real.

“when she received the messengers and sent them out another way?”

When Joshua sent spies into Jericho, Rahab hid them, protected them from the king’s men, and helped them escape (Joshua 2:1–21). She had confessed faith in Israel’s God: “the LORD your God, He is God in heaven above and on earth beneath” (Joshua 2:11). Her protective actions gave visible expression to the allegiance to Israel’s God that she had confessed. James commends the actions he names. He does not approve every detail of her story.
25.notes: Hebrews 11:31 also commends Rahab: “By faith the harlot Rahab did not perish with those who did not believe, when she had received the spies with peace.”

26.brief: “For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.” James closes the argument by showing that faith and its works belong together as surely as body and spirit in a living person.
26.explain:
“For as the body without the spirit is dead,”

James closes the argument with a picture. When the spirit leaves the body, the body dies. It may still look like a person, but there is no life in it.

“so faith without works is dead also.”

A faith that produces no works has no life in it. It may look like faith, use the language of faith, and claim the name of faith, but it is lifeless. James closes the argument by showing that faith and its works belong together as surely as body and spirit in a living person. The comparison does not mean that works create faith. It means that genuine faith and its works cannot be separated.
26.notes: This is the third time in the chapter that James calls faith without works “dead” (2:17, 20, 26).
